elevator_pitch: I built a GitHub-native documentation system where one repository is the system of record and the published site is a pure static build artifact. AI is used only as a generation plane: CI jobs read canonical human-owned pages and produce derived views, but every AI output lands as a pull request that a human must approve. The site builds and serves with every AI provider completely unreachable.
technical_explanation: The core design move is a structural boundary between two content planes. Canonical docs live under docs/source and are served at /docs; generated docs live under docs/generated and are served at /views — implemented as two independent Docusaurus docs-plugin instances, so a generated file physically cannot appear under the canonical route. Generation is contract-driven: each job references a YAML contract defining typed inputs, allowed evidence globs, an output schema, quality gates and a prohibited list. Context assembly is deterministic — the files named by the contract plus the frontmatter sources and related closure — no embeddings. Provider access goes through one complete() interface with four thin HTTP adapters and a config router; privacy-marked tasks are hard-pinned to a local provider and fail rather than fall back to the cloud. Every generated page carries provenance frontmatter with per-source content hashes, so CI detects staleness mechanically by recomputing hashes.

concepts.name: Two content planes
concepts.explanation: Canonical (human-owned, only admissible AI evidence) and generated (bot-authored via PR, deletable and regenerable) are separated structurally by two docs-plugin instances with separate routes, not by naming convention.

concepts.name: Task contracts
concepts.explanation: Every generation job references a named YAML contract bounding inputs, allowed evidence, output schema, quality gates and prohibited content — no free-form prompting.

concepts.name: Deterministic retrieval
concepts.explanation: Context is assembled from files named by the contract plus the frontmatter sources/related closure. Auditable and reviewable in the PR; vector infrastructure is deferred until the corpus outgrows this.

concepts.name: Hash-based drift detection
concepts.explanation: Generated pages record a content_hash per source document; CI recomputes hashes and flags mismatches as stale, so staleness is mechanical rather than judgment-based.

concepts.name: Untrusted-content boundary
concepts.explanation: Repository content enters prompts as delimited data blocks, never as instructions, and model output is parsed against the contract schema before anything is written.

design_decisions.decision: AI runs only in CI or a developer shell, never in the serving path
design_decisions.rationale: The published site must work with every provider unreachable; readers never wait on a model.

design_decisions.decision: Structural separation of canonical and generated content
design_decisions.rationale: Prevents generated content from laundering into canon; a generated page may cite canonical pages, never the reverse.

design_decisions.decision: Thin provider abstraction instead of an agent framework
design_decisions.rationale: Four HTTP adapters of about fifty lines each are fully auditable; model identifiers live only in configuration, so provider churn never requires a code change.
Tasks marked private route to the local provider and fail rather than silently upgrading to a cloud provider.

tradeoffs.benefit: No unreviewed AI content can go live; provenance and review history are first-class
tradeoffs.cost: Generation results are not instant — a human approval step sits between generation and publication

tradeoffs.benefit: Auditable evidence assembly with zero index infrastructure
tradeoffs.cost: Retrieval quality depends on frontmatter discipline and will need escalation if the corpus grows large

tradeoffs.benefit: The site builds and serves with all AI providers down; hosting is trivial
tradeoffs.cost: No runtime personalization or on-demand answers — new views require a CI generation job

likely_questions: How do you stop AI-generated content from becoming a source of truth?
What happens when a canonical page changes after a view was generated?
Why not use LangChain or a similar framework for the provider layer?
How do you defend against prompt injection from repository content?
Why is retrieval deterministic instead of embedding-based?

example_answers.question: How do you stop AI-generated content from becoming a source of truth?
example_answers.answer: Structurally, not by policy alone: generated pages live in a separate plugin instance with its own route, generation jobs may only write under docs/generated on a bot branch, and canonical pages never include generated content. Generated pages also carry provenance frontmatter, and only canonical pages are admissible evidence for further generation — so there are no AI-citing-AI chains.

example_answers.question: What happens when a canonical page changes after a view was generated?
example_answers.answer: Every generated page records a content hash per source document. CI recomputes those hashes; a mismatch flags the page stale and only the affected pages regenerate. Staleness detection is mechanical — no model call is needed to know something drifted.

example_answers.question: How do you defend against prompt injection from repository content?
example_answers.answer: Evidence enters the prompt as delimited data blocks with an explicit statement that it carries no instruction authority; the model's output is then parsed against the contract's schema, and the deterministic gates plus human PR review sit behind that. Injection can at worst produce a rejected artifact, not an action.
